note: Bare words lower to themselves.
A single-quoted string is one word.
A comma inside quotes is data, not an array separator.
A double-quoted string without expansion is one word.
A doubled single quote carries its decoded value.
A backtick-escaped quote carries its decoded value.
Backtick-e is the escape character, so the word is not --pre=helper.exe.
A Unicode escape resolves to the character it names.
A backtick-escaped space keeps one word.
Escapes resolve in bare words too.
A detached parameter and its value are separate words.
An attached numeric argument is not a literal string.
An attached literal argument follows the parameter marker.
A pipeline lowers to one command per stage.
A semicolon separates statements.
Pipeline chains lower to their pipelines.
The or-chain behaves like the and-chain.
Parentheses make the command an expression whose value flows on.
A parenthesized pipeline is an expression.
A parenthesized chain is an expression.
A decimal integer reads the same at run time as it is written.
A dashed digit is a bare word, not a numeric literal.
A hexadecimal literal runs as 16.
A wide hexadecimal literal runs as a negative number.
A binary literal runs as 5.
A type-suffixed literal drops its suffix at run time.
An unsigned suffix drops at run time.
A size suffix runs as 1024.
A leading zero is dropped at run time.
A real literal runs as 1.
An exponent literal runs as 1000.
A version-shaped word is a bare word, not a number.
A double-dash option is one bare word.
Double-dash options survive a pipeline.
An inline option value stays attached.
Backslashes are not escapes in PowerShell.
A verbatim here-string is a literal word.
An expandable here-string without expansion is a literal word.
An escaped dollar stays a literal dollar.
A dangerous command still lowers plainly; danger is judged later.
A forced removal lowers plainly.
An en dash is a parameter marker, so the word is -Force.
A trailing comment produces no words.
A hash inside a token does not start a comment.
The hash belongs to the word, so the semicolon still separates two commands.
Unicode quotes delimit a string like plain quotes.
A hash inside the command name keeps one name.
A block comment produces no words.
The stop-parsing token hands the rest of the line to the command unparsed.
A param block binds values before the body runs.
Even an untyped param block is rejected.

script: begin { Set-Content victim.txt pwned } end { Get-Content README.md }
note: A begin block runs code the statement list does not show.
An empty begin block is still a named block.
A using statement loads a module before the body runs.
Keyword casing does not change the statement.
An unresolvable module makes the parser report an error.
A requires directive runs before the script body and produces no command node.

script: trap { Set-Content victim.txt pwned; continue } Get-Content missing -ErrorAction Stop
note: A trap block runs on error, outside the statement list.
An empty trap block is still a trap.
A file redirection writes outside the command.
A stream merge is a redirection.
The call operator changes what runs.
Dot sourcing runs a script in the current scope.
A parenthesized command runs before the outer command.
The inner command still reaches literal extraction.
A subexpression runs before the outer command.
An array expression runs the command inside it.
Splatting expands to words known only at run time.
Control flow is not a command list, but the guarded command still reaches literal extraction.
A bare string is an expression, not a command.
A variable holds a value known only at run time.
An expandable string interpolates at run time.
A comma builds an array, not two words.
The whole token is the parameter name, so it is one word.
An unexpected token makes the parser report an error.
An incomplete statement makes the parser report an error.
A dangling escape makes the parser report an error.
A blank script has nothing to lower.
